title: Cellular telephony from incompatible analog systems to interoperable digital GSM-scale networks
pressure: Mobile telephony faced scarce spectrum, handoff, billing, roaming and infrastructure cost; national analog systems risked small incompatible markets.
preExistingWorldModel: Cellular frequency reuse and switching concepts existed, but implementations differed by country, spectrum and vendor regime.
observationsAndInstruments: NMT demonstrated cross-border regional mobile service.
European coordination developed GSM as a common digital system.
GSM standardized radio/network interfaces and roaming while countries coordinated spectrum/deployment.
Multiple suppliers and rapid adoption expanded the system beyond Europe.
decisiveTests: capacity/spectrum efficiency and billing/authentication improve over analog
technicalOrScientificTransition: Cellular scale depended on network architecture plus standards, spectrum, roaming and supplier ecosystems; interoperability could create more system value than isolated local optimization.
rivalsAndFailures: No single cellular standard dominated globally.
Standardization traded local design freedom for larger interoperable markets.
A capable handset without coverage, roaming and tariffs had little standalone value.
diffusionAndScaling: Diffusion depended on complements, cost/yield/standards and institutional adoption; the nominal breakthrough date did not equal broad effective use.
standardsAndInstitutions: Laboratories, firms, standard bodies, regulators, users and infrastructure operators owned different parts of evidence, implementation and consequence.
externalitiesAndCorrections: Lifecycle harms and authority changes are preserved where evidenced rather than inferred from local technical success.
secondOrderEffects: Cellular scale depended on network architecture plus standards, spectrum, roaming and supplier ecosystems; interoperability could create more system value than isolated local optimization.
sourceNativeSummary: Cellular scale depended on network architecture plus standards, spectrum, roaming and supplier ecosystems; interoperability could create more system value than isolated local optimization.
